findings.title: Flagship hero 'worked example' contradicts the engine and the site's own public /read page — directions swapped
findings.detail: The hero panel (marketing.ts HERO_READING) is hardcoded HTML labeled 'Worked example', with a code comment (marketing.ts:137-141) claiming 'the panel cannot drift away from what the app would say on /pair/ENTP/INFP'. It has drifted: the row 'ENTP → INFP | Examined | 44 | Your leading function lands on their Blind spot; you can flatten them without noticing' (marketing.ts:150-157) and 'INFP → ENTP | Examiner | 34' (marketing.ts:160-167) attach each score and gloss to the wrong side. Engine introspection this session: relation(ENTP,INFP)=SR 'Examiner', ease(ENTP,INFP)=34, gloss 'THEIR leading function lands on YOUR Blind spot'; relation(INFP,ENTP)=SV 'Examined', ease(INFP,ENTP)=44. Stack check confirms the physical fact: INFP's lead Fi sits in ENTP's Blind spot (seat 6); ENTP's lead Ne sits in INFP's Support (seat 1) — so INFP is the oblivious 'flattener' with the easier 44, and ENTP carries the 34. The same site's own public SEO page agrees with the engine and against the hero: curl of /read/entp-and-infp renders 'ENTP experiences it as 34/100 effortful, INFP experiences it as 44/100 ... INFP has the easier time of it.' The hero's footer ('only one of them can feel it', marketing.ts:170-172) therefore points readers at the wrong person. For a brand whose one page-level claim is 'Nothing can quietly contradict anything else' (marketing.ts:663-664), the front door contradicting its own public reading page on its flagship example is the exact failure mode the positioning stakes itself against — discoverable by any enthusiast in two clicks. tests/marketing.test.ts pins '128/128', 'r −0.15' and '$25' as strings (lines 36-45) but nothing pins the hero panel's direction mapping.
findings.evidence: src/worker/marketing.ts:137-173; engine outputs run this session: ease(ENTP,INFP)=34 / ease(INFP,ENTP)=44, relation(ENTP,INFP)='Examiner', INFP lead Fi in ENTP seat 6 'Blind spot', ENTP lead Ne in INFP seat 1 'Support'; curl http://localhost:5173/read/entp-and-infp ('ENTP experiences it as 34/100 effortful, INFP ... 44/100'); tests/marketing.test.ts:36-45; screenshot home-signedout-desktop-light.png (hero panel top-right shows ENTP→INFP 44)
findings.recommendation: Swap the two direction labels in HERO_READING (44/Examined/its gloss belongs to INFP → ENTP; 34/Examiner to ENTP → INFP), and add a marketing test that renders marketingPage() and asserts each row's score equals ease() for the direction its label names — the same discipline tests/cards.test.ts already applies to the deck.

findings.title: Paying customers are promised 'straight in' but /signin tells them they will wait for owner approval
findings.detail: The pricing card promises 'Checkout via Stripe. Payment unlocks your account automatically — sign in with Google right after and you're straight in' (marketing.ts:807-810), and stripe.ts does implement automatic preapproval on a settled checkout (stripe.ts:124-152 → preapprove()). But the /signin gate a payer actually lands on says the opposite: 'This is a private instrument. Sign in to continue. ... Access is granted by the owner of this deployment. If you sign in with Google you will wait until they approve you' (curl of /signin this session; screenshot signin-desktop-light.png). There is no 'already paid?' acknowledgment anywhere on the gate, and in the dev deployment no Google button renders at all — only an Access code field — so the only visible path is the invite code the visitor does not have. The moment of maximum buyer anxiety (just paid $25, hit a wall labeled 'private instrument') gets copy written for the invite-only posture, not the self-serve one the marketing page sells.
findings.evidence: src/worker/marketing.ts:807-810; src/worker/stripe.ts:124-152; curl http://localhost:5173/signin visible-text extract ('you will wait until they approve you'); screenshot signin-desktop-light.png (Access code field only, no Google button, no mention of payment)
findings.recommendation: Add one sentence to the /signin gate: 'Just subscribed? Sign in with Google using the email you paid with — payment unlocks your account automatically.' Render it (and the Google button) whenever Stripe + Google are configured; keep the owner-approval sentence only for the non-payer path.

findings.title: Hero CTA promises 'Eight either-or questions' free; /onramp delivers two, behind a required email gate, and never shows the promised 'directional reading'
findings.detail: The hero cta-note reads 'Free, no account. Eight either-or questions, no scoring you can fail' (marketing.ts:596). The /onramp funnel it links to asks only TWO of the eight real coin questions (answersFrom() reads only q0 and q4, onramp.ts:131-136; header comment onramp.ts:50-52 says 'Two of the questions read real coins'); the rest are a Likert hook, a friction checklist and interstitials. The email step is titled 'See your directional reading.' (onramp.ts:359) with a required email input (onramp.ts:366) — but the done step delivers no directional reading of any kind, only 'Your pattern is one of about N of the sixteen' plus a $25 CTA (onramp.ts:384-393), and the emailed 'explainer' (leads.ts:285-303) is the same one-of-N sentence with a 'Start now — $25/user·mo' button. Three promises ('eight questions', 'no account'/free result without giving anything, 'see your directional reading') are each broken in sequence, which is precisely the pattern the page's own copy attacks in competitors ('Tools that promise more than this are overpromising', marketing.ts:783).
findings.evidence: src/worker/marketing.ts:594-596; src/worker/onramp.ts:50-52,131-136,359,366,384-393; src/worker/leads.ts:285-303
findings.recommendation: Make the copy tell the truth about the funnel: 'Free two-minute teaser — two of the eight questions, watch the field narrow' — or make the funnel honor the copy by asking all four determining coins (calculate() already supports it) so the done page can show a genuinely narrowed result; retitle the email step to what it delivers ('Get the two-minute explainer by email').

findings.title: The 136 public /read pair readings — the site's best free proof — are linked from nowhere in the marketing funnel
findings.detail: read.ts serves fully public, crawlable, engine-derived readings for every pair and type ('the two ease scores as a headline', read.ts:10-36); /read and /read/entp-and-infp both return 200 anonymously with real directional scores. This is exactly the try-before-buy proof the front page's claims need — a live demonstration of 'both directions, derived'. But grep of marketing.ts finds zero links to /read: the nav (marketing.ts:512-519) and footer (552-560) list Product / Who it's for / Pricing / Compared / Partners / Sign in only. A visitor unwilling to pay $25 sight-unseen has no discoverable way to see one real full-ish reading; the surface exists purely for search crawlers via sitemap.xml (read.ts:447-449). The onramp done page likewise sells the $25 plan without ever showing a sample reading (onramp.ts:383-393).
findings.evidence: src/worker/read.ts:10-36,445-467; curl: GET /read → 200, GET /read/entp-and-infp → 200 with 'ENTP experiences it as 34/100'; grep '"/read' src/worker/marketing.ts → no matches; src/worker/marketing.ts:512-519,552-560
findings.recommendation: Add 'Sample readings' to the nav/footer and a 'See a real pair reading, free →' link under the hero panel and on the onramp done page — the asset is already built, tested, and on-message; it just needs to be reachable by humans, not only crawlers.

findings.title: Proof band's '27% of pairs differ by direction' is not reproducible from the band's own definition and is pinned by no test
findings.detail: The proof band says '256 ordered pairs, each scored twice' followed by '27% of pairs differ by direction' (marketing.ts:607-608). Engine sweep this session: 64 of 256 ordered pairs are asymmetric = 25.0%; 32 of 136 unordered = 23.5%. The 27% is only recoverable as 64/240 = 26.7% (excluding the 16 self-pairs), a denominator the band never states — and the adjacent stat has just told the reader the universe is 256. Meanwhile two of the band's five numbers ARE genuinely test-pinned and reproduced (tests/ingested.test.ts:55-58 asserts 128/128; :214 asserts r ≈ −0.154; 61/61 tests passed this session), which makes the un-pinned 27% the soft spot an adversarial enthusiast will find. Also '256 ordered pairs, each scored twice' double-counts: each ordered pair is scored once; it is the 136 unordered pairs that get two scores.
findings.evidence: src/worker/marketing.ts:606-611; engine sweep output: 'ordered pairs: 256 asymmetric: 64 = 25.0%; unordered pairs: 136 asymmetric: 32 = 23.5%'; npx vitest run tests/ingested.test.ts → 61 passed; tests/marketing.test.ts:36-45 (pins 128/128 and r −0.15 strings, not 27%)
findings.recommendation: Either restate as '1 in 4 ordered pairs differ by direction' (25%, matching the stated 256 universe) or '27% of cross-type pairs', and add a marketing test that derives the figure from ease() the way ingested.test.ts derives 128/128; fix 'each scored twice' to '136 pairings, each scored in both directions'.

findings.title: No og:image or twitter:image on any public page — shares of a visually distinctive product render as bare text
findings.detail: siteHead() emits og:type/title/description/url/site_name and twitter:card 'summary' but no og:image or twitter:image (marketing.ts:487-506, confirmed by grep: no matches for og:image in marketing.ts). The product's whole aesthetic argument — the discs, the worked-reading panel, the seals — is invisible in the one context (a shared link) where a first impression is decided. The favicon is a data: URI SVG (marketing.ts:30-37), so there is not even a logo fallback most scrapers can use.
findings.evidence: src/worker/marketing.ts:487-506; grep 'og:image\|twitter:image' src/worker/marketing.ts → no matches
findings.recommendation: Serve a static /og.png (the hero worked-reading panel or the eight-disc alphabet band rendered at 1200×630) from the worker and add og:image + twitter:card 'summary_large_image' to siteHead(); pin its presence in tests/marketing.test.ts alongside the existing metadata assertions.

findings.title: Partner terms doc says 'thirteen-stage course'; the public page and the product say fifteen
findings.detail: PARTNERSHIP-TERMS.md:35 describes 'a thirteen-stage course', while the public marketing page says 'fifteen-stage course' twice (marketing.ts:693, 802) and the curriculum actually contains 15 stage slugs (src/learn/curriculum.tsx, 15 slug entries counted this session; Home.tsx:88 renders STAGES.length dynamically). A partner doing diligence who reads both documents finds the confidential terms understating the public claim — small, but this doc opens by declaring its numbers 'fixed until 31 December 2026' (PARTNERSHIP-TERMS.md:4), which makes stale facts inside it read as either carelessness or a different product version. The doc's other quantitative claims check out where verifiable (103-term lexicon is pinned by tests/plain.test.ts:30; 128/128 and r ≈ −0.15 reproduced by tests/ingested.test.ts; $25/25%/$18/$15/$12-20k/$750+$12/$36k figures match partner-rate-card.html exactly).
findings.evidence: docs/PARTNERSHIP-TERMS.md:4,35; src/worker/marketing.ts:693,802; src/learn/curriculum.tsx (15 stage slugs listed via grep this session); tests/plain.test.ts:28-30; docs/partner-rate-card.html:155-203,235-256
findings.recommendation: Update PARTNERSHIP-TERMS.md to 'fifteen-stage' (and audit its other prose counts against the code on each release); consider generating such counts into the doc the way the deck derives card copy, since stale numbers in a 'fixed until 2026' document are disproportionately damaging.

findings.title: The crown-jewel fact — 256 directed scores derived at runtime from ~2KB of seed, no database, no stored matrix — is quantified only in a confidential partner doc
findings.detail: The public page's version of the differentiator is soft: 'computed from one small piece of structure, never looked up in a table' (marketing.ts:661-663) and the meta description's 'one small piece of structure' (marketing.ts:176-179). The arresting, concrete form — 'The structure is derived at runtime from roughly 2 KB of seed data. There is no database and no stored matrix. The structural tables cannot drift apart, because they are computed' — appears only in PARTNERSHIP-TERMS.md:43-45, a document marked confidential. 'Derived' is above the fold as an adjective, but the falsifiable, memorable quantity that makes an enthusiast stop scrolling never reaches the public surface, while the proof band spends its five slots on counts (16/256/27%) that any lookup-table competitor could also print.
findings.evidence: src/worker/marketing.ts:176-179,606-611,656-664; docs/PARTNERSHIP-TERMS.md:43-45; screenshot home-signedout-desktop-light.png (proof band shows 16/256/27%/128-128/r−0.15, no seed-size or no-database claim)
findings.recommendation: Give the derivation claim one proof-band slot in its concrete form — e.g. '~2 KB · the seed everything is computed from — no stored matrix' — and verify the figure with a test that measures the actual seed tables, so the number is as pinned as 128/128.

findings.title: Validation claims cite deliberately unnamed sources, leaving the strongest trust signals unfalsifiable to outsiders
findings.detail: The proof band's best items — '128/128 agreement with an independent published table' and 'the survey matrix that disagrees, shipped anyway' (marketing.ts:609-610) — name no source, per the stated positioning rule 'No third-party system, author or trademark is named' (marketing.ts:10-11), enforced repo-wide by tests/attribution.test.ts (referenced at tests/marketing.test.ts:89-90). PARTNERSHIP-TERMS.md:49-58 repeats the same claims equally unnamed ('An independent published 16-pattern table', 'One published survey matrix'). Internally these are real (ingested.test.ts reproduces both), but an enthusiast or a partner's diligence reviewer cannot distinguish them from invented benchmarks — 'we agree with a table we won't name' reads as the same rhetorical move the page condemns in others. The /compare page shows the no-naming rule is scoped, not absolute: it names MBTI, Socionics and the Big Five (curl this session: title 'Octant compared — MBTI, Socionics and the Big Five').
findings.evidence: src/worker/marketing.ts:9-12,606-611; docs/PARTNERSHIP-TERMS.md:49-58; tests/marketing.test.ts:88-91; tests/ingested.test.ts:55-58,214; curl http://localhost:5173/compare → title names MBTI/Socionics/Big Five
findings.recommendation: Since /compare already breaks the naming seal deliberately, add a short public 'Validation' note (or a /compare section) that names the ingested sources and links the test file names, so the honest-asterisk culture is checkable rather than asserted; at minimum name the sources in the partner materials, where diligence is the whole point.

findings.title: Hero proof panel leans on undefined jargon for the newcomer's first ten seconds
findings.detail: The first thing a newcomer must parse in the hero is 'ENTP · INFP', two unlabeled colored discs (Ne, Fi), relation names 'Examined'/'Examiner', and 'Blind spot' — none defined before use (marketing.ts:142-173). The alphabet caption beneath speaks in the palette's own language: 'indigo N, sienna S, verdigris T, madder F · ripples break out for e, in for i' (marketing.ts:77), which is legible only after the course. The headline and lede are excellent plain language; the proof panel then costs newcomers exactly the comprehension the lede just bought. Enthusiasts, by contrast, parse it instantly — the panel is well aimed at them.
findings.evidence: src/worker/marketing.ts:71-77,142-173; screenshot home-signedout-desktop-light.png (hero panel and alphabet caption visible above the fold)
findings.recommendation: Add one plain-language line inside the panel ('Two people, one relationship, scored from each side') and simplify the caption to 'The eight habits of mind every reading is spelled in' — keep the color vocabulary for the course.

findings.title: Two different taglines: the public page sells 'Compatibility runs in two directions', the app a convert enters is titled 'Read the wiring'
findings.detail: Public title and h1: 'Octant — compatibility runs in two directions' (marketing.ts:175,587). The gated app's document title is 'Octant — read the wiring' (index.html:6) and the signed-in Home hero is 'Read the wiring.' (Home.tsx:39). The promise a buyer just paid for (directional compatibility) is not the headline of the product they enter; the directional claim survives inside signed-in Home only as band 1 ('EASE RUNS BOTH WAYS', Home.tsx:211-233). The onboarding does bridge well — /welcome's final screen is exactly the marketing claim ('One number would have quietly picked a side', Welcome.tsx:83-92) — so this is a naming split, not a substance split.
findings.evidence: src/worker/marketing.ts:175,587; index.html:6; src/views/Home.tsx:39,208-233; src/views/Welcome.tsx:83-92; screenshot home-signedin-desktop-light.png (actually /welcome step 1, confirming onboarding entry)
findings.recommendation: Pick one flagship phrase for both doors, or make the signed-in Home's first band the directional-ease claim so the just-converted buyer immediately sees the thing they bought.

findings.title: Partner rate card uses a different brand accent than every other surface
findings.detail: partner-rate-card.html sets --accent:#5B32A8 (line 25) and draws its logo dot in #5B32A8 (lines 139, 224); the marketing site, onramp, favicon and mark all use #4C4899 (marketing.ts:21,34-36,203; onramp.ts STYLE:417). The rate card is the single artifact partners forward internally, and it is the one surface in a different violet. Everything else about the card is unusually consistent with PARTNERSHIP-TERMS.md — every price, minimum, floor and rollover term matches line for line.
findings.evidence: docs/partner-rate-card.html:25,139,224; src/worker/marketing.ts:21,34-36,203; src/worker/onramp.ts:417; cross-check of all figures against docs/PARTNERSHIP-TERMS.md sections 3-6
findings.recommendation: Change the rate card's --accent and logo fill to #4C4899 (or document #5B32A8 as the deliberate print-optimized variant in the design system so it stops looking like drift).

marketing.scoreRationale: The marketing architecture is unusually strong for a solo product: a sharp, differentiated wedge claim ('a single compatibility score is a fiction') stated identically across the landing page, onramp interstitials, nurture emails and partner docs (FRICTION_COPY reused verbatim, leads.ts:231-262); a real no-invite path (free /onramp → Stripe $25 → webhook auto-preapproval, verified in stripe.ts); pricing that is consistent to the dollar across five surfaces; a proof band whose two hardest claims (128/128, r −0.15) are actually reproduced by the test suite; partner materials with diligence-grade candor (P1-P5 premises, the non-negotiable no-hiring clause); and a genuinely good CSS-only mobile treatment. But the execution has one disqualifying wound and several self-inflicted trust leaks: the flagship hero worked example has its two directions swapped relative to the engine AND to the site's own public /read page — falsifying the page's central 'nothing can quietly contradict anything else' claim on its own front door — the /signin gate tells paying customers the opposite of what pricing promised, the hero CTA overpromises what /onramp delivers three separate ways, and the best free proof surface (136 public readings) is unlinked from the funnel. For a brand built entirely on derived consistency and honest asterisks, these are category errors, not polish gaps; fixing the P0 and three P1s would move this to an 8+.
marketing.strongestThing: The proof band's honest-asterisk item — 'r −0.15 · the survey matrix that disagrees, shipped anyway' (marketing.ts:610) — is real marketed evidence backed by CI: tests/ingested.test.ts:214 asserts the correlation ≈ −0.154 and :55-58 derives the 128/128 agreement, and the whole file passed 61/61 when run this session; tests/marketing.test.ts:38-41 then pins both strings into the page. Marketing copy that advertises its own disconfirming evidence and reproduces it in the test suite is a genuinely rare trust asset for the enthusiast and partner lenses — preserve it and extend the same test-pinned discipline to the band's other numbers.
marketing.notes: Verified this session (commands run, not quoted from docs): ease(ENTP,INFP)=34 / ease(INFP,ENTP)=44; INFP lead Fi in ENTP's Blind spot seat, ENTP lead Ne in INFP's Support seat; asymmetric ordered pairs 64/256=25.0% (64/240=26.7% if self-pairs excluded — the likely origin of the marketed '27%'); npx vitest run tests/ingested.test.ts → 61/61 passed (reproduces 128/128 and r≈−0.154); 15 course stage slugs in src/learn/curriculum.tsx; lexicon 103 pinned by tests/plain.test.ts:30; anonymous route statuses on the live dev server: / 200 (marketing HTML), /signin 200, /onramp 200, /partners 200, /compare 200, /read 200, /read/entp-and-infp 200, /pricing 401, /waitlist 401, /reading/ENTP-INFP 401. Unverified: PARTNERSHIP-TERMS.md's 'two independently-keyed intertype charts agree on all 256 cells each' and the wheel-layer claims (plausibly inside the 61 passed ingested tests but not individually confirmed); the '~2 KB seed' size itself (quoted from the partner doc, not measured). Drift found: 'thirteen-stage' in PARTNERSHIP-TERMS.md:35 vs fifteen in code/marketing; rate-card accent #5B32A8 vs site #4C4899; hero worked-example direction swap (the big one). Screenshot caveats: 'home-signedin-desktop-light.png' actually captures /welcome step 1 (first-sign-in onboarding), so the signed-in Home.tsx was audited from source only; no mobile screenshots existed — mobile behavior of the signed-out page was verified in code only (CSS-only details/summary menu ≤860px at marketing.ts:271-322, stacked full-width CTAs ≤560px at :331-335), and both desktop light/dark screenshots render correctly. Funnel mechanics verified in code: Stripe payment link → checkout.session webhook → preapprove(email) → Google sign-in (stripe.ts), onramp lead capture is abuse-gated by a signed start token with a 2s minimum (onramp.ts:86-98), and the nurture sequence honors its own opt-in split (leads.ts:14-23,141-180). The signin gate's owner-approval copy and missing Google button reflect this dev deployment's config; production may render the Google button, but the contradictory copy is unconditional in the template.

findings.title: Marketing hero's flagship worked example attaches both scores/labels opposite to the app's own direction convention
findings.detail: The hero panel (served on anonymous GET /) shows 'ENTP → INFP · Examined · 44' and 'INFP → ENTP · Examiner · 34'. The engine says ease(ENTP,INFP)=34 and REL[ENTP][INFP]=SR ('Examiner' — INFP examines ENTP). Every in-app surface attaches ease(a,b) to a's experience: PairReader labels ease(target,persp) as '[target] being around [persp]', Matrix titles cells 'ease v for t'. So on /pair/ENTP/INFP the app prints 'ENTP being around INFP' = 34, while the marketing row headed 'ENTP → INFP' prints 44. The panel is only coherent under an unstated receiver-perspective arrow convention no app surface uses. Worse, the row bodies reuse REL_DEF's second-person glosses ('Your leading function lands on their Blind spot') under headings naming two third parties — the exact two-pronoun defect plain.ts:48-60 documents fixing in-app with SLOT_ABOUT. The in-code comment claims the panel 'cannot drift away from what the app would say on /pair/ENTP/INFP' — it already disagrees with that page. A diligent partner or enthusiast who checks the numbers (the product's whole pitch is that you can) finds the front door contradicting the app.
findings.evidence: src/worker/marketing.ts:137-173 (hardcoded panel + 'cannot drift' comment); served output confirmed via curl http://localhost:5173/ ('ENTP → INFP / Examined / 44'); engine output via npx tsx: REL[ENTP][INFP]=SR, ease(ENTP,INFP)=34, ease(INFP,ENTP)=44; src/views/PairReader.tsx:111-115 ('${target} being around ${persp}'); src/views/Matrix.tsx:92 ('ease ${v} for ${t}'); src/engine/plain.ts:48-60 (two-pronoun rationale)
findings.recommendation: Rebuild the hero panel from ease()/REL_NAME at build time (or copy the app's exact labeling: 'ENTP being around INFP — Examiner across from you — 34'). Replace second-person REL_DEF text with slotAbout-style named-party copy. Add a marketing test asserting the two numbers appear beside the same party-labels the app uses.

findings.title: Every pair page's 'The short version' opens with the old borrowed relation name, contradicting the shipped name shown two lines below
findings.detail: REL_FRAME — the first sentence of every composed playbook — still carries six pre-rename names: 'Identity.', 'Activity.', 'Mirror.', 'Business.', 'Super-Ego.', 'Conflict.' The shipped vocabulary (REL_NAME, live per VOCABULARY.md §2 status) is Twin, Spark, Opposite hand, Colleague, Standoff, Headwind. On a pair page the playbook panel renders first, so a reader sees 'Conflict. Your strongest function lands…' directly above an Explain saying the relationship's name is 'Headwind'. Two names for one relation, inches apart, one of them ('Super-Ego', 'Duality-family' socionics naming) exactly the borrowed vocabulary VOCABULARY.md §4/§10 exists to keep out — it slips the attribution test because that test bans authors/systems, not relation names. The curriculum has the same slip: stage 10 labels rel-cf 'Conflict' after stage 6 taught 'Counterpart/Damper/Standoff'.
findings.evidence: src/engine/data.ts:257-274 (REL_FRAME: 'Identity.', 'Activity.', 'Mirror.', 'Business.', 'Super-Ego.', 'Conflict.') vs src/engine/data.ts:96-113 (REL_NAME: Twin/Spark/Opposite hand/Colleague/Standoff/Headwind); src/engine/playbook.ts:24 (parts[0] = REL_FRAME[code]); src/views/PairReader.tsx:71-83 (playbook panel above REL_NAME Explain); src/learn/curriculum.tsx:681 (<Term id="rel-cf">Conflict</Term>) vs curriculum.tsx:408-410; docs/VOCABULARY.md §4, §10; tests/attribution.test.ts:50-65 (ban list covers authors/systems only)
findings.recommendation: Update REL_FRAME's six stale lead-ins to the REL_NAME terms (or derive the lead-in from REL_NAME programmatically so they cannot diverge), fix curriculum.tsx:681 to 'Headwind', and extend the attribution/vocab test to assert REL_FRAME's first word matches REL_NAME.

findings.title: Marketing CTA promises the free onramp is 'Eight either-or questions'; it delivers two, plus a flattery hook and an email gate mislabeled 'See your directional reading'
findings.detail: Under the hero button the note reads 'Free, no account. Eight either-or questions, no scoring you can fail.' The /onramp flow behind it asks 2 of the 8 coin questions (q0, q4), a persuasion Likert ('I can usually tell within a few minutes how someone is "wired"'), a goal-segmentation question, a pain-point multi-pick, and an email capture headed 'See your directional reading' — after which no reading appears, only 'Your pattern is one of about N of the sixteen' plus a $25 CTA. The done-step copy is honest ('a directional read from two of the eight questions'), but that honesty arrives after the email is collected. The funnel's tone also inverts the instrument's: the calculator says 'Self-report is the weakest evidence in typology… read two or three of the closest fits rather than trusting the number', while the funnel affirms 'That's exactly where seeing the mechanism… does the most work.' This is the one surface where the honest-asterisk culture breaks.
findings.evidence: src/worker/marketing.ts:594-596 (CTA + 'Eight either-or questions' note); src/worker/onramp.ts:160-192 (only q0 and q4 are coin questions), 170-173 (hook1 Likert), 356-374 ('See your directional reading' email step), 376-393 (done step, $25 CTA); tone contrast: src/views/Calculator.tsx:209-212 vs onramp.ts:177-182
findings.recommendation: Make the CTA note describe what's actually behind it ('Free two-minute teaser — two of the eight questions; the full read is in the product'), retitle the email step to what it does ('Get the two-minute explainer by email'), or let the onramp ask all eight coins and gate only the mechanism. Cut or reframe the flattery Likert.

findings.title: Three collective nouns for the same grouping live simultaneously: 'quadra', 'Camp', and 'Clubs'
findings.detail: Home says 'grouped by quadra or temperament'; the course stage is titled 'Clubs and temperaments' but its body teaches 'quadra' (Explain: 'A quadra is the set of four types…'); two stages later the bonds stage says 'exactly one such mesh exists per Camp' and 'Your Camp's one mesh'; the type page header chip prints 'Alpha Camp'; the plain gloss for quadra opens 'A Camp: four types that trust the same four tools.' VOCABULARY.md documents the camps rename (Hearth/Forge/Market/Field) as pending — but the interim state is not the old term consistently, it's three terms interleaved across consecutive course stages, which reads as three different concepts to a newcomer and as carelessness to an enthusiast.

The copy craft here is unusually strong: a written doctrine (plain first, technical underneath) that is actually implemented as a component (Explain), enforced by tests (plain coverage, jargon bans, attribution bans, marketing string pins), with humane error copy, honest uncertainty notes in the course, and comparison pages that concede real ground. Grade-4 plain glosses sit above grade-10 mechanics exactly as promised. But the audit found the doctrine's trust layer cracked in three places that matter most: the public hero's flagship worked example attaches both direction scores opposite to the app's own labeling convention (in a product whose one pitch is 'check our numbers'), every pair page opens its playbook with a stale borrowed relation name that contradicts the shipped name two lines below, and the marketing CTA misdescribes the free funnel while the funnel itself breaks the product's honesty register. findings.title: [security] Onramp lead-capture token is replayable: one aged token can mail Octant-branded email to unlimited arbitrary addresses and burn the KV write budget
findings.detail: The anti-abuse token for the public /onramp funnel is seal({t: now}) — it carries only its issue time, is not bound to the submitted email, is not single-use, and lives 1 hour (START_TTL_SECONDS=3600, MIN_COMPLETION_MS=2000). verifyStartToken (onramp.ts:94-98) checks only signature + age >= 2s. So a script mints one token via a single GET, waits 2 seconds, then replays that same token with any number of different email= values. Each new email triggers captureLead: up to 2 KV writes (leads.ts:90,96 — against the free tier's 1,000 writes/day noted at wrangler.jsonc:75-77) plus one outbound Octant-branded Resend explainer email to an address the attacker chose (leads.ts:91-93) — the exact sender-reputation/spam-complaint risk the in-source comment names. The comment (onramp.ts:63-84) acknowledges 'two requests with a sleep between them still works' and defers IP rate limiting, but understates the exposure: it is not two requests per victim, it is one mint plus N replays for N victims. LOGIN_LIMITER and CHAT_LIMITER exist as cross-isolate bindings (wrangler.jsonc:116-119); no limiter covers this path. This accepted risk was priced when the funnel was hypothetical; with the marketing site, Stripe checkout and nurture sequence now live, it is the front door.
findings.evidence: src/worker/onramp.ts:63-98 (token design + comment); src/worker/leads.ts:78-101 (captureLead: KV write + sendMail per new email); wrangler.jsonc:75-77 (KV write-budget note), 116-119 (limiters exist for login/chat only); curl http://localhost:5173/onramp → 200 anonymous this session
findings.recommendation: Make the start token single-use per capture (include a nonce and record it briefly in LEADS, or bind the token to the email at the email step and verify the binding at done), and/or add an ONRAMP_LIMITER ratelimit binding keyed on cf-connecting-ip — the binding mechanism is already proven in this codebase and costs nothing.

findings.title: [a11y] No skip link: keyboard and screen-reader users traverse 12 nav tabs plus 4 icon buttons before reaching content on every page
findings.detail: App.tsx renders the masthead (12 NavLinks from TABS at lines 24-37, then 4 icon buttons at 137-171) before <main> with no skip-to-content mechanism. grep for 'skip' across src/App.tsx, src/main.tsx and all of src/styles returns nothing. findings.title: [a11y] SPA route changes neither move focus nor announce the new page — navigation is silent to assistive tech
findings.detail: The navigation effect (App.tsx:67-77) scrolls to top or to a hash target but never moves focus and there is no aria-live route announcer anywhere in the app (grep for aria-live across src/ finds only the gate page's error message region, auth.ts:450, and role="status" on the calculator dock and chat spinner). In an SPA, a click on 'Matrix' produces no screen-reader feedback that anything happened; focus remains on the clicked nav link while the entire main region has been replaced. This is the canonical client-side-routing accessibility gap, and QA-REVIEW §4 already concedes 'Screen-reader announcement in an actual reader' is untested — this is the concrete defect that test would have caught.
findings.evidence: src/App.tsx:66-77 (scroll-only navigation effect); grep 'aria-live' src → only src/worker/auth.ts:450 (gate page) — no app-side live region (this session); docs/QA-REVIEW.md:122 (§4 admits the gap)

findings.title: [a11y] Chat assistant answers stream into a container with no live region — replies are never announced

findings.title: [perf] One 632KB/195KB-gzip chunk, zero code splitting; every view statically imported — and the bundle grew 13% in 3 weeks with nothing watching it
findings.detail: Verified: src/App.tsx:3-22 imports all 16 views statically (no React.lazy anywhere in src — grep confirms), and vite.config.ts's build block is `{ outDir: "dist", sourcemap: false }` with no manualChunks/rollupOptions. The one chunk is 632,308 B raw / 195,377 B gzip (measured), up from QA-REVIEW's 558KB/178KB on 2026-08-01. Honest split assessment from source sizes: the heaviest modules — engine/lexicon.ts (89,148 B) and learn/curriculum.tsx (48,307 B) — are NOT cleanly splittable (lexicon is imported by Term.tsx which renders everywhere; curriculum by Home.tsx), but TypeReader.tsx (46,034 B source, one route), Guide.tsx (14,422 B), Matrix, and Admin.tsx (6,350 B, owner-only) are route-isolated and lazy-loadable today. Counterweight the fix must respect: under run_worker_first every extra chunk request is a billable Worker invocation (wrangler.jsonc:30-35), so splitting into many small chunks pulls against the platform economics — a handful of route chunks, not fine-grained splitting, is the right shape. At invite-only scale this is P2 not P1; it becomes user-facing the day a paid signup from the funnel hits the app shell on a phone.
findings.evidence: ls -la dist/assets → index-B4qwz5m7.js 632308 B; gzip -c | wc -c → 195377 (both this session); src/App.tsx:3-22 (static imports); vite.config.ts:107 (build block); wc -c src/views/*.tsx and src/engine/* src/learn/* (sizes above); import graphs via grep (engine/lexicon ← Term.tsx:3; curriculum ← Home.tsx:6); docs/QA-REVIEW.md:16 (558KB baseline)
findings.recommendation: React.lazy the four route-isolated heavy views (TypeReader, Guide, Matrix, Admin) behind the existing ErrorBoundary/Suspense, cap it there given the invocation economics, and add a bundle-size assertion test so the next 13% is a decision.

findings.title: [a11y] role="img" flattens data-rich diagrams to one-sentence labels; the sr-only fallback pattern exists but is applied inconsistently
findings.detail: The codebase's own best practice: NetworkRing pairs role="img" with a visually-hidden per-edge list because '<title> inside role=img' is mouse-only (NetworkRing.tsx:80, tests/a11y.test.tsx:44-59 asserts it), and OctagramWheel's aria-label is a generated full-sentence describe(wheel) (OctagramWheel.tsx:81-82). But WiringSchematic — the flagship figure — collapses eight seat assignments rendered as SVG <text> to the static label 'The eight function seats of ENTP, from Lead down to Dread' (WiringSchematic.tsx:47-52): role="img" hides the child text from AT, so which function sits in which seat is not announced by the figure itself (recoverable only if surrounding page text duplicates it). Same pattern risk applies to OctagramMap and BondFigure/MutualLanding/RelationLanding (role="img" with short labels, verified via grep). This is P3 not P2 because every SVG in src/components does carry at least role="img"+aria-label or aria-hidden (verified across all 21 svg-bearing files this session) — the floor is high; the ceiling is uneven.
findings.evidence: src/components/WiringSchematic.tsx:47-56 (label vs. rendered seat text); src/components/NetworkRing.tsx:80 + src/styles/base.css:127-140 (the existing sr-only pattern); src/components/OctagramWheel.tsx:78-82 (describe()); per-file svg/aria audit via grep this session (21 files, no unlabeled SVG found)
findings.recommendation: Apply the NetworkRing pattern to WiringSchematic (an sr-only ordered list of the eight seats is derivable from the same props), or generate a describe()-style sentence as OctagramWheel does.

findings.title: [perf] Asset serving has no cache policy under run_worker_first — every reload re-invokes the Worker for revalidation, and the documented trigger for fixing it has arguably fired
findings.detail: wrangler.jsonc:30-42 states the tradeoff with unusual candor: run_worker_first: true makes every asset request a billable invocation, accepted as 'a rounding error' for 'an invite-only instrument with a handful of readers', with the fix (long immutable TTLs on fingerprinted assets) deferred until 'this ever opens up'. Since that was written, the deployment grew a public marketing site, an ad-traffic quiz funnel (onramp.ts:28-30 explicitly anticipates 'anonymous ad traffic'), Stripe checkout, and an SEO surface with a sitemap — i.e., the open-up trigger is partially pulled: paid conversions land signed-in on the un-cached 632KB app shell. No _headers file exists in dist/ and headers.ts deliberately never touches cache-control (headers.ts:65-67). The fingerprinted filename (index-B4qwz5m7.js) makes an immutable TTL trivially safe, and browser caching is per-already-authenticated-user so the wall is unaffected — AR-2's own reasoning.
findings.evidence: wrangler.jsonc:30-42 (read this session); ls dist/ → no _headers; src/worker/headers.ts:65-67 ('never touches… existing cache-control'); docs/QA-REVIEW.md:143-149 (AR-2 with the trigger condition); src/worker/onramp.ts:28-30 (ad-traffic intent)
findings.recommendation: Ship AR-2's own recommendation: cache-control immutable max-age on /assets/* responses (settable in the Worker after env.ASSETS.fetch, keeping headers.ts's no-touch rule for everything else), and watch the invocation graph as the comment prescribes.

findings.title: [perf] Font chain: three Google-hosted families on the critical path of both the gated app and the public marketing pages; self-hosting is also the named path to a tighter CSP

Cost: a third-party DNS+TLS+CSS+font waterfall on first paint for every visitor including anonymous funnel traffic, and a privacy/GDPR talking point (Google Fonts IP transmission) that diligence reviews raise. headers.ts:26-28 already records that self-hosting 'would be the one change that lets this tighten to self alone' for style-src/font-src — the CSP currently carries style-src 'unsafe-inline' https://fonts.googleapis.com and font-src https://fonts.gstatic.com (observed live this session). The owner's call is documented ('owner's call, 2026-08'), so this is a priced decision, not an oversight — flagged because two improvements (perf waterfall, CSP tightening) share the one fix.
findings.evidence: index.html:8-10 and dist/index.html (same, read this session); src/styles/tokens.css:15-17 (fallback stacks); src/worker/headers.ts:26-28,51-52; live CSP header captured via curl this session
findings.recommendation: Self-host the three families as woff2 in /assets (they are all OFL-licensed), drop the two Google hosts from the CSP, and keep display=swap via @font-face.

findings.title: [security] Dev server serves the SPA shell without the security header layer — CSP breakage of the app is invisible until deployed
findings.detail: In dev, the Worker's ASSETS.fetch returns a passthrough marker and vite.config.ts hands the request to Vite's own pipeline (vite.config.ts devApi: 'if (out.headers.get(PASS)) return next()') — which bypasses withSecurityHeaders entirely. Verified live: authenticated GET /type/ENTP on localhost:5173 returns no CSP/XCTO/referrer-policy headers, while the Worker-rendered marketing page on the same server carries the full set including the three-hash CSP. Consequence: a change that violates the CSP inside the React app (a new inline script, an external fetch) sails through `npm run dev` and every test, and first fails in a deployed browser — which is why QA-REVIEW's manual checklist item 8 exists. Dev-only, by construction; noted because the repo's stated philosophy is 'the SAME Worker in dev that runs in production' (vite.config.ts header comment) and this is the one seam where that promise doesn't hold.
findings.evidence: curl -D - http://localhost:5173/type/ENTP (authed) → no security headers vs curl -D - / → full CSP (both this session); vite.config.ts:44-100 (PASS marker + next()); docs/QA-REVIEW.md:208-209 (checklist item 8)
findings.recommendation: In the dev middleware, when the passthrough fires for an HTML/document request, still apply withSecurityHeaders to Vite's response (or at minimum inject the CSP meta) so CSP violations surface in dev consoles.

findings.title: [a11y] Onramp quiz radio groups lack fieldset/legend; question prompt is not programmatically bound to its options
findings.detail: The public funnel's answer options are correctly label-wrapped radios (verified live: <label class="choice"><input type="radio" name="goal" …>), but there is no <fieldset>/<legend> grouping, so a screen-reader user tabbing into the radio group hears option text without the question it answers. The gated app's equivalent (Calculator) uses aria-pressed toggle buttons with visible question context instead (Bits.tsx:124-139 ChoiceCard) — a different, acceptable pattern. Low severity: one question per page and the heading precedes the group, so context is recoverable by reading order; still a cheap conformance win on the page type most likely to be a stranger's first contact.
findings.evidence: curl 'http://localhost:5173/onramp?step=1&goal=self' markup captured this session (label+radio, no fieldset/legend in output); src/components/Bits.tsx:124-139 (the app-side pattern for contrast)
findings.recommendation: Wrap each step's options in <fieldset> with the question as <legend> (styling reset is 3 lines of CSS) in onramp.ts's step renderer.

findings.title: [security] Minor hygiene: signInProblem strips <>& instead of using the existing escapeHtml; Google error strings are currently all-internal so exposure is nil
findings.detail: index.ts:362 interpolates the OAuth failure message into HTML via message.replace(/[<>&]/g, "") — an ad-hoc strip, while the codebase's real escaper (escapeHtml, used by auth.ts:501 and leads.ts:221) sits unused here. Audited every error string completeGoogleSignIn can return (google.ts:109-161): all are fixed literals; the one branch keyed on a user-controlled query param (error=access_denied) selects between two fixed strings rather than echoing input. So there is no injection today — this is a latent-footgun note: the sanitizer at the sink is weaker than the house standard, and a future error message that embeds a Google-supplied string (error_description is the classic) would rely on it. Filed at P3 precisely because the current code is safe; it costs one identifier to make the sink match the rest of the Worker.
findings.evidence: src/worker/index.ts:349-366 (signInProblem); src/worker/google.ts:107-161 (all error strings enumerated this session); src/worker/html.ts escapeHtml used at auth.ts:501, leads.ts:221
findings.recommendation: Replace the regex strip with escapeHtml(message) in signInProblem.

supporting.notes: Evidence base: all file:line citations were read this session from /home/user/octant; all measurements run this session against the repo and the dev server at localhost:5173 (authenticated via the provided cookie where noted). Key verified numbers: npx vitest run → 1225 tests / 47 files, all passing; dist/assets/index-B4qwz5m7.js = 632,308 B raw / 195,377 B gzip (dist built this session), CSS 22,864 B / 5,430 B gzip; npx biome lint src → 5 warnings (base.css:121-123 noImportantStyles ×3, components.css:394 and 483 noDescendingSpecificity), matching the orchestrator's stated drift figures independently. QA-REVIEW baseline figures (832 tests, 558KB, 0 warnings, two CSP hashes) are quoted from docs/QA-REVIEW.md:11-16,36 as the DOCUMENT's claims, not re-verified against the 2026-08-01 commit — the drift deltas are the finding. REVIEW-FINDINGS.md is correctly self-marked as a superseded historical snapshot (its own header), so I did not treat its counts as open claims; QA-REVIEW is the live document and is the one drifting. Reconciliation of QA-REVIEW open items — verified still open this session: M6's two overclaiming test names (engine.test.ts:180, lexicon.test.ts:194-200 with the always-true quadra guard), AR-2 asset cache policy (no _headers, no cache-control on assets), shots.mjs absent from ci.yml, AR-8 OAuth token-exchange leg untested (no token-endpoint mock in google-auth.test.ts), and §4's real-AT keyboard/screen-reader gap (no playwright/axe in package.json). Nothing QA-REVIEW marked fixed was found regressed: rate-limit bindings present and fail-open-tested (ratelimit.test.ts:42-49), error boundaries in App.tsx:178,209, headers layer at the single exit, chat context validation tests present, logout-only-on-ok at App.tsx:87-92. Security items examined and found sound (deliberately not filed as findings): Stripe webhook verification (stripe.ts:44-61 — timestamp tolerance, multi-v1 acceptance, constant-time compare; retry-safe 500 on KV failure at :145-149), session HMAC design and constant-time comparison discipline (crypto.ts:58-67 used consistently), admin owner-gating (index.ts:186-192 resolves owner server-side per request; admin.ts signed links are single-person, GET-shows/POST-decides), export token via digest comparison (export.ts:103-111), codeId identity fix for bare-code chat history (auth.ts:157-164, index.ts history routes scope by who). Secrets scan of dist found only env-var NAMES in Admin UI copy, no values. Claims I could NOT verify from here and did not assert: production run_worker_first edge behavior (platform-only, as QA-REVIEW itself states), real Cloudflare invocation billing, actual screen-reader behavior (no AT available in this environment — announcement findings are derived from the DOM/ARIA semantics, which is the standard basis but not a live NVDA/VoiceOver pass). The P1 (onramp token replay) is a source-level proof of capability — I did not send actual emails or flood KV to demonstrate it. One caution for synthesis: the dev server's missing security headers on the SPA shell is a dev-only parity gap, not a production hole — production shell responses flow through withSecurityHeaders; do not let it get summarized as 'app has no CSP'.
supporting.scoreRationale: The supporting dimensions are unusually strong for a project of this size, which is why one P1 and a cluster of P2s still leave a 7.5. Accessibility floor is far above typical: every one of the 21 SVG-bearing components carries role=img+aria-label or aria-hidden (audited individually), mouse-only affordances have deliberate sr-only/text fallbacks with tests asserting them, interactive controls are native elements with correct states (aria-pressed choice buttons, native select, aria-expanded menu, Escape handling), and prefers-reduced-motion, focus-visible, and scrollable-region focusability are all handled — but the three SPA-era gaps (no skip link, silent route changes, unannounced chat streaming) are exactly the ones that make the app hard to actually use with a screen reader, so the polish exceeds the plumbing. Security posture is the best dimension: fail-closed wall ordered before assets, one header layer with a hash-pinned CSP, constant-time comparison discipline in a single shared module, correct hand-rolled Stripe verification with retry-safe failure semantics, and tests that assert failure postures — undermined one notch by the replayable onramp token on the now-live public funnel and by the QA review's adversarial coverage lagging the public surface it vouches for. Performance is unoptimized but consciously priced (632KB single chunk, no asset caching, Google fonts — each with a written tradeoff), and the growth-without-a-budget pattern plus the partially-fired AR-2 trigger keep it from being fully excused. The docs-drift theme is the real deduction: this repo's differentiator is that its documents are load-bearing, and the load-bearing one (QA-REVIEW) went stale on every gate within three weeks, including a pre-deploy check that now cries wolf.
supporting.strongestThing: The single-exit security architecture and its honesty about failure modes — preserve it exactly. Every response leaves through withSecurityHeaders at the router's one exit (src/worker/index.ts:57-64), the CSP pins its three inline scripts by recomputed hash so drift fails the suite rather than the page (src/worker/headers.ts:31-62, tests/headers.test.ts:29-55), all secret comparisons route through one constant-time module (src/worker/crypto.ts:58-67), the wall fails closed with the reasoning written at the decision site (auth.ts:17-38, wrangler.jsonc:16-42 — including the billing cost of run_worker_first stated rather than waved away), and the tests assert postures most suites never touch: a rate-limiter OUTAGE failing open on purpose (tests/ratelimit.test.ts:42-49), a malformed-context flood not charging the shared budget (ratelimit.test.ts:98-127), a webhook KV failure returning 500 specifically so Stripe redelivers (stripe.ts:145-149). This is diligence-grade engineering because the accepted risks are in the source next to the code they price — the audit's job was mostly checking whether reality still matched the writing, which is the highest compliment a codebase can earn.
